grammar.title: 2B: Present perfect + for / since, present perfect continuous
grammar.explanation:
We use **have/has + past participle** with **for** (a period of time) or **since** (a point in time) to talk about something that started in the past and is still true now. This is the classic way to describe job tenure or the remuneration you have earned over the years.

We ask about unfinished periods with **How long + have/has ...?**. Never use the present simple here — "How long do you try" is wrong when the effort to break the glass ceiling is still going on.

We use the **present perfect continuous** (**have/has been + verb-ing**) for actions that started in the past and are still happening, or that have just finished with visible results. A manager who has been onboarding new staff all week, or micromanaging every detail until burnout, fits this form perfectly.

With non-action verbs like know, believe, or have, use the present perfect simple — never the continuous. You can say you have known about nepotism for years, but not "have been knowing."

**Live** and **work** are flexible — both forms work with the same meaning. You can say you have worked in a meritocracy since 2015, or that you have been working there, just as naturally.

The simple form stresses the result or how many times something happened; the continuous stresses the ongoing activity. A whistleblower who has exposed fraud twice this year is a result; one who has been preparing a report all week is an activity. The same split applies to headhunt: five engineers headhunted this year, or months spent headhunting.
examples: She *has held tenure* at the university since 2018. (for/since + still true now)
How long *have you been fighting* the glass ceiling in this industry? (How long + unfinished period)
They *have been onboarding* new engineers since March. (continuous for an ongoing action)
He *has been micromanaging* his team for months, and they are close to burnout. (continuous stresses the activity)
They *have known* about the nepotism for years. (non-action verb + present perfect simple)
She *has worked* in a true meritocracy since 2015. (work in either form)
She *has been working* in a true meritocracy since 2015. (same meaning)
The agency *has headhunted* five engineers this year. (simple stresses the result)
They *have been headhunting* for months without success. (continuous stresses the activity)
A whistleblower *has exposed* the fraud twice, and her remuneration was cut. (simple + result)

practice.q: Why is 'They have known about the nepotism for years' correct, but 'They have been knowing about it for years' wrong?
practice.a: 'Know' is a non-action verb, so it cannot take the continuous form. Non-action verbs always use the present perfect simple here.

practice.q: Complete the sentence: 'She ___ (work) here since 2019 — she loves the fair remuneration.'
practice.a: 'has worked' or 'has been working' — with live and work, both forms are correct with the same meaning.

practice.q: Which sentence stresses the activity itself: 'She has written three reports' or 'She has been writing reports all morning'?
practice.a: 'She has been writing reports all morning' — the continuous form stresses the ongoing activity, while the simple form stresses the result.
